title: Paul Appeals to Caesar
summary: The new governor, Festus, hears Paul's case in Caesarea. When Festus proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul, knowing the danger there, uses his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to the emperor. Before he can be sent, King Agrippa and Bernice visit Festus, who lays out the puzzling case and arranges for Agrippa to hear Paul himself.
story: Two years have passed since Felix left Paul in custody (24:27). A new governor gives Paul's accusers a new opening, and they revive the plan to ambush him on the road to Jerusalem (compare 23:12-15). The decisive event of the chapter is Paul's appeal to Caesar in verse 11. With those words the legal road to Rome opens: the promise of 23:11, that Paul must testify in Rome, now has a Roman legal mechanism behind it. The second half of the chapter sets the stage for Paul's longest defense speech, before Agrippa, in chapter 26.
historical:
Porcius Festus succeeded Felix as governor of Judea, most likely about AD 59 or 60 (the date is debated). He governed only briefly; Josephus reports that he died in office, and the lawless interval before the next governor arrived saw the high priest execute James, the brother of Jesus, in about AD 62. Festus seems to have tried to act fairly and quickly, but he was new, needed the goodwill of the Jerusalem leaders, and did not understand Jewish religious disputes.

King Agrippa is Herod Agrippa II, son of the Agrippa who executed James son of Zebedee and died in Acts 12. He ruled territories to the north and east of Galilee under Roman favor, and Rome gave him oversight of the Jerusalem temple, including the power to appoint the high priest. That made him the natural person for a Roman governor to consult on a Jewish religious case. Bernice was his sister; she lived with him for long periods after the death of her husband, and she later became the companion of the future emperor Titus. The emperor to whom Paul appealed was Nero, who reigned from AD 54 to 68. His later persecution of Christians came after this, and the early years of his reign had a reputation for sound government.
cultural:
A Roman citizen accused on a serious charge had the right to have his case heard by the emperor's court rather than a provincial governor's. Scholars debate the exact legal procedure in the first century, but Acts presents the essential point clearly: once Paul appealed, and Festus had consulted his council of advisers, the governor could no longer simply hand him over or try him in Jerusalem. The appeal was a real risk for Paul. It meant a long voyage, an uncertain wait, and a hearing before a court whose decisions could not be undone. He made it because Festus's offer to move the trial to Jerusalem put him back within reach of the men who had sworn to kill him.

Festus's report to Agrippa shows how the case looked to a Roman. He had expected a crime; instead he found a dispute about the accusers' own religion (the word can mean religion or superstition, and Festus is probably being careful before a Jewish king) and about a certain Jesus who had died but whom Paul said was alive. Festus also faced an administrative problem. A governor forwarding a prisoner to the emperor had to send a written statement of the charges, and he had nothing definite to write. The grand hearing before Agrippa, with its pomp, military commanders, and city leaders, was partly a way to get expert help with that letter.
literary: The chapter has two scenes, and the second retells the first. In verses 1-12 Luke narrates the hearing directly; in verses 13-22 Festus summarizes it for Agrippa, and in verses 24-27 he summarizes it again for the assembled court. The repetition lets the reader hear Paul's case through a Roman official's eyes, and each retelling adds to the chapter's theme: no one can prove the charges, and the governor himself finds nothing worthy of death (verse 25). Luke has placed similar verdicts throughout the trial sequence (23:29, 26:31-32), echoing the repeated declarations of Jesus's innocence by Pilate in Luke's Gospel. The crisp exchange of verses 11-12, “I appeal to Caesar” and Festus's reply, is the hinge of the whole section.

outline.t: Festus refuses to move the case to Jerusalem
Festus explains the case to Agrippa
Paul is brought before Agrippa and Bernice

doctrines.note: A Roman legal right, used at the right moment, becomes the means by which God's promise to bring Paul to Rome is carried out. Scripture often shows God working through ordinary institutions rather than around them.

Paul stands before governors and kings, as Jesus said his witnesses would (Luke 21:12-13). The chapter sets the kingdoms of this world, with their pomp and procedures, beside the claim that the crucified Jesus is alive.

Paul says he does not refuse to die if he has done wrong, but he will not be handed over unjustly. Christian willingness to suffer is not the same as passivity; Paul uses lawful means to protect himself.

words.note: Epikaleo, to call upon or appeal. Elsewhere in Acts it describes calling on the name of the Lord for salvation (2:21, 22:16). Here it is the legal term for Paul's appeal to the emperor. The same verb covers both appeals, though Luke draws no explicit connection.

Bema, the judgment seat, the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate gave rulings. Paul says he is standing before Caesar's judgment seat, since the governor judges in the emperor's name. Paul uses the same word for the judgment seat of God and of Christ (Romans 14:10, 2 Corinthians 5:10).

Sebastos, revered or august, the Greek equivalent of the Latin title Augustus, used here as a title for the reigning emperor. It carried a religious tone, since emperors were honored with cults across the eastern provinces.

Kurios, lord or master. Festus calls the emperor our lord in verse 26, a title increasingly used of emperors in this period. Christians confessed that Jesus is Lord, and the overlap would later become a point of conflict.

christ: Festus sums up the whole dispute in one telling phrase: it concerned a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive (verse 19). A Roman governor, with no stake in the question, identifies exactly what the gospel is about. Christianity stands or falls not on a teaching but on whether a crucified man is alive. The chapter also continues Luke's parallel between Paul and Jesus: both are handed between a Roman governor and a Herodian ruler (Luke 23:6-12), both are declared innocent, and both are kept in custody anyway. Paul walks the road his Lord walked, but his Lord now walks it with him as the living one Festus could not explain.
questions: Paul used his rights as a citizen to avoid an unjust trial. When is it right for a Christian to use legal protections, and when might it be right to give them up?
Festus could only describe Jesus as a man who died whom Paul said was alive. How would you explain to an outsider why that claim matters so much?
Festus wanted to do the Jews a favor, as Felix had. How does the wish to please powerful people bend a person's sense of justice?
